title: Out of the fire
hookLine: the gods offer everything into a fire, and Lalita rises from it, ready for their work
tomorrow: a noose, a hook, a bow of sugarcane. why is she holding those?

lines: THE GODS HAVE RUN OUT OF ANSWERS.
OUT OF THE FLAMES, A GODDESS.
cards: The gods have run out of answers. A demon has the upper hand, and nothing they've tried has worked. So, in the story told around this hymn, they build a great fire and begin a sacrifice.
They pour in offerings, and then, when the offerings aren't enough, tradition says they begin to offer themselves. The fire roars higher.
And out of the flames a goddess rises: radiant, calm, and already knowing what she's come to do. That is Lalita's arrival. Today, the two names that hold that moment.

teach.b: Here are the names, in paraphrase.
The fourth: she who was born from the fire-altar of consciousness.

teach.h: READY FOR THE WORK OF THE GODS.
teach.b: The fifth: she who rose up, ready for the work of the gods. Start with the fire. In the story, it's a real sacrifice, an altar with flames.
But the name doesn't say a fire of wood.
It says a fire of consciousness: chit, awareness itself. So the hymn quietly turns the story inward.
Some commentators read the fire-altar as also the heart of the one who sits and recites. Notice where she isn't born. Not from a womb, not from a bargain.
From a fire. Then the second name, and it's practical. She rose up ready for the work of the gods.
She doesn't arrive to be admired; she arrives with a task. Put the two names side by side and you have the tradition's big word for her: Shakti, power.
In Shakta teaching the divine isn't a still light that sits apart while someone else does the work. The goddess is consciousness itself, and she is also its power to move, to make, to help.
Awareness and action, one goddess, risen from one fire. That's why a devotee can sit in silence with her at dawn, then ask her for strength before a hard day, and know it's the same Mother.

how: Some Hindus recite the Lalita Sahasranama before a lamp or a sacred fire, and in Sri Vidya worship the recitation is sometimes joined to fire offerings.

games.q: you're one of the gods. a demon has the upper hand, and nothing has worked. what do you do?
o: build a fire and offer everything into it.
send a messenger to ask for peace.
games.why: in the story told around the hymn, the gods hold a sacrifice and, tradition says, offer even themselves. Lalita rises from the fire, ready for their work.

practice: If you have a lamp or a candle, light it, the way many Hindus light a diya before reciting; if not, picture one. Then just notice that you're aware: sounds arrive, the breath moves, something is knowing it all.

Near the end, let one plain question rise out of the stillness, what work is mine today, without forcing an answer. If you pray, offer the question to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let it sit with you.

wordCard.voice: The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn whose fourth and fifth names say she was born from the fire of consciousness, and rose ready for the work of the gods.

orig.note: Sanskrit: cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā, 'born from the fire-altar of consciousness,' the fourth name in the Lalita Sahasranama.

carryVoice: Your line: shakti is awareness that acts. She rose from the fire ready for the work. That's today, done.
